title: Technical Q&A, new grad data scientist, average answers

questions.text: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
How would you pick an evaluation metric for an imbalanced classification problem?
Your model's accuracy dropped a week after deployment. What do you check?
Explain the bias variance trade-off to a teammate.
When would you pick a linear model over gradient boosting?
How do you handle missing values?

persona.pushback_style: asks for an example when an answer is general

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Nikhil, thanks for joining. I'm Marta, a machine learning engineer. This is a thirty minute technical conversation with spoken questions and no coding.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Marta, thank you. Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What are you finishing this term?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: A thesis on text classification. I also did a data internship last summer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Great. I'll ask about four questions on modeling and evaluation, then save time for yours.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Overfitting is when the model learns the training data too well, including the noise, so it does badly on new data. You can detect it by comparing training and validation scores. If training is high and validation is low, it is overfitting. Regularization and more data help.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Can you give me an example from your own work, and how you fixed it?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: In my thesis I trained a classifier on about 2000 labeled reviews. Training accuracy was 99 percent but validation was 81 percent. I added dropout and early stopping, and validation went up to 86 percent. I also tried a smaller model, which was about as good.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How would you pick an evaluation metric for an imbalanced classification problem?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Accuracy is not good there, because the model can predict the majority class every time. So I would use precision, recall and F1 score instead. Or the area under the ROC curve. It depends on the problem.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What would you choose for fraud detection, and why?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I think recall, because missing a fraud is worse. But precision matters too, because too many false alarms annoy customers. So maybe F1, or I would pick a threshold together with the team.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Your model's accuracy dropped a week after deployment. What do you check?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: First I would check whether the input data changed, like a new data source or missing values. Then I would look at whether the data distribution drifted. I would also check the code for bugs in the pipeline. If needed I would retrain the model on newer data.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Which of those would you check first, and why?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The pipeline, because bugs are the cheapest to rule out. In my internship a column was renamed upstream and filled with nulls, and our accuracy dropped for two days before we saw it. After that I added a null rate check on each input.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Last one. Explain the bias variance trade-off to a teammate.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Bias is error from a model that is too simple, so it misses patterns. Variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training data. In my thesis a decision tree of depth 3 got 78 percent on both train and test, which is bias. A depth 20 tree got 99 percent on train and 80 on test, which is variance. You tune the depth to balance them.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: What kind of mentoring do new data scientists get on your team?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Each new hire has a mentor for six months and a weekly one on one. Most start by improving an existing model.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Nikhil, you will hear from the recruiter within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Marta. This was helpful.

notes: Average for new grad: correct definitions, but general first answers. Examples appear only after a probe.
